opus-5.5.text:
Rainblood was a huge thing for me. I first played it when I was still in school, and it was one of those moments where something clicked. Before that, I sort of assumed that games worth caring about came from big studios in Japan or the US, with huge teams and budgets. Then here was this game made basically by one person in China, with RPG Maker, and it had such a strong atmosphere: dark, wuxia-flavored, a bit gothic, with a story that didn't talk down to you. It felt personal, like an auteur work.

What it really shaped was my sense of what was *possible*. It told me you don't need permission to make something. If you have a clear aesthetic and the stubbornness to finish it, an individual voice can cut through. I remember reading forum posts about how it was made and thinking, okay, this is a craft I could actually learn, not some distant industrial process.

It also taught me something about taste. Rainblood wasn't trying to be everything. It committed fully to a mood, to a certain kind of Chinese martial-arts melancholy, and that commitment is what made it memorable. Later, whenever I worked on my own projects, I'd come back to that: what is the one feeling this thing should leave you with, and am I protecting that feeling or diluting it?

And honestly, it gave me some cultural confidence. It showed that stories rooted in our own traditions could feel cool and modern, not old-fashioned. That idea, that you can take something deeply local and make it resonate more widely, has stayed with me ever since.

r001.rationale: The candidate says Rainblood made Kay Ke think game-making was a craft they could learn and showed that an individual voice could cut through, conveying inspiration to create original work.

r002.rationale: The candidate mentions reading forum posts about how Rainblood was made, but does not describe looking to admired creators’ paths as guides for pursuing creative aspirations.

fable-5.1.text:
Honestly, Rainblood was the first time I realized that a game could be made by one person, and that it could still hit me as hard as anything from a big studio. I played the original Rainblood: Town of Death when I was a student, and it had this wuxia atmosphere, this black-and-white ink style with that stark red, and a story that was dark and personal in a way I hadn't seen in Chinese games before. What really got me was finding out afterward that Liang Qiwei basically built it alone, with RPG Maker, in his spare time. That cracked something open for me.

Before that, I thought making games was something that happened somewhere else, in Japan or the US, with hundreds of people and huge budgets. Rainblood made it feel reachable. If someone could pour their own aesthetic, their own obsessions, into a small project and have people respond to it, then maybe I could too. So I started tinkering, learning tools, making tiny things nobody played.

The second thing it gave me was a sense that Chinese cultural material, wuxia, ink painting, that whole mood, didn't have to be a gimmick. Rainblood took it seriously, and that gave me permission to draw on things that felt like mine rather than imitating what was popular overseas.

And then watching the series grow, from the first game to Mirage, to Rainblood Chronicles and eventually Bloody Spell, it taught me something less romantic too. It showed how hard that path is, how a one-person vision has to turn into a team, and how much gets compromised or stretched along the way. So Rainblood shaped both my ambition and my realism. I wanted to make something with that kind of personal fingerprint, and I also learned early that keeping that fingerprint intact as you grow is the actual challenge.

r001.rationale: Kay says Rainblood made game creation feel reachable and led them to think “maybe I could too,” then start making small projects.

r002.rationale: Kay points to Liang Qiwei’s solo development and Rainblood’s later growth as examples that shaped their own creative ambitions and understanding of the path.

astra-6.text: Rainblood made me want to create something of my own. What drew me in was how the atmosphere, the story, and the visual style felt like parts of the same world. It made me think about the kind of work I wanted to make—something personal, with a distinct identity, that might leave someone else feeling the way I felt playing it.
